teaser: A woman king borrows a lion's body, and a style that was already four centuries old.
review_notes:
IMAGE: the photo shows the Met's small limestone maned sphinx (acc. 31.3.94, usually titled 'Hatshepsut as a Maned Sphinx'), not the colossal granite 'Sphinx of Hatshepsut' (31.3.166). The lesson is written about the limestone sphinx shown.
Length given as roughly one meter; check Met dimensions.
Smooth pale areas described as modern plaster restoration, colored and rough areas as original stone.
Chest inscription read as 'Maatkare, beloved of Amun, given life forever' per the Met.
Reign dates c. 1479-1458 BC; destruction about 20 years after her death under Thutmose III.
Original placement (a pair flanking the upper ramp at Deir el-Bahri) follows the Met's reconstruction.

lesson.text: One thousand years. That is roughly how old the Great Sphinx of Giza already was when this small sphinx was carved, around 1470 BC. For the person who ordered it, a sphinx was a deeply traditional image. Which was exactly why she wanted one.

Her name was Hatshepsut. She was a king's daughter and a king's widow, and she began by ruling on behalf of her young stepson. Then, within a few years, she took the full titles of pharaoh for herself and held them for about two decades.

Egypt had no word for a ruling queen and no images for one. A pharaoh was male by definition. So Hatshepsut's sculptors gave her the ancient kit of kingship, piece by piece, and a sphinx, a lion with a human head, was among the oldest pieces available.

lesson.title: Half animal, all king
lesson.text: This sphinx is more lion than most. Follow the head from the top down.

spots.title: Lion's ears
spots.text: Round animal ears stand where human ones would be. The Great Sphinx wears a royal headcloth. Here the sculptor kept the lion's own ears and mane, so only the face is human.

spots.title: The mane
spots.text: A stiff ruff frames the face, its fur drawn as fine cut lines. The warm orange patches are original painted surface: the whole statue was once colored.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Wide eyes, a small firm mouth, a pointed chin. Hatshepsut's statues share this delicate, slightly catlike face. On the forehead, a stump remains from the royal cobra.

spots.title: The beard
spots.text: A long false beard, strapped on by kings at ceremonies. On a woman it was not a disguise. It was a badge of office, like a crown.

lesson.text: That mane was a quotation. Sphinxes with a lion's ruff had been made for kings of the Twelfth Dynasty, some four hundred years earlier, an age Egyptians looked back on as a classic. By copying their look, Hatshepsut claimed a place in their line.

The sphinx is a patchwork. The smooth, pale areas are modern plaster, filling gaps between the surviving chunks of limestone. The broken, darker surfaces, like the rough front of the base, are the ancient stone.

It is in pieces because someone wanted it gone. About twenty years after Hatshepsut died, her stepson Thutmose III had her statues dragged out of her temple at Deir el-Bahri, near modern Luxor, smashed, and dumped in nearby pits.
The smashing was thorough, but it missed something. Egyptians believed a name carried a person's existence. Erase the name and you erase the king. On this sphinx, her name is still there.
Hatshepsut's name is carved somewhere on the lion's body. Where would a sculptor put it so that everyone approaching could read it?

spots.title: On the chest
spots.text: Between the forelegs, just under the tip of the beard, faint hieroglyphs sit inside an oval ring that marks a royal name. They give her throne name, Maatkare, “beloved of Amun.”

lesson.text: Amun was the great god of Thebes, and her temple was built facing his across the Nile. This sphinx, about a meter long, was probably one of a pair guarding the upper ramp. Much bigger ones, carved in granite and weighing tons, lined the approach below.

Archaeologists from the Metropolitan Museum dug the fragments out of the dumps in the 1920s. Pieces of the same statues had already been carried off to other countries, and matching them up took years of patient jigsaw work.

Why did Thutmose III wait twenty years? Hatred seems unlikely after so long. Many historians now think he was clearing the record so that his own son would inherit without a rival branch of the family, and without the precedent of a woman on the throne.
Hatshepsut did not invent a new image for a female king. She took the oldest images of power in Egypt and put her own face and name on them.

quiz.question: What makes this sphinx unusual compared with the Great Sphinx?
options: It keeps a lion's mane and ears around the human face
quiz.explanation: Only the face is human: the ears and ruff belong to the lion.

quiz.question: Why did Hatshepsut copy a four-hundred-year-old style?
options: To link herself to admired earlier kings
Because her sculptors knew no other
quiz.explanation: The maned sphinx quoted the Twelfth Dynasty, an age Egyptians saw as classic.

quiz.question: Who had her statues smashed?
quiz.explanation: He ordered the destruction about twenty years after her death.

quiz.question: What are the smooth, pale parts of the statue?
quiz.explanation: Restorers filled the missing areas between ancient fragments with plaster.

quiz.question: Where is her name carved?
options: On the chest, between the forelegs
On the back of the head
quiz.explanation: A ring enclosing her throne name, Maatkare, sits under the beard.

facts.text: The false beard was meant to hide the fact that Hatshepsut was a woman.
facts.explanation: It was a badge of kingship worn at ceremonies, not a disguise.

facts.text: The Great Sphinx of Giza was already about a thousand years old in Hatshepsut's time.
facts.explanation: This sphinx dates from around 1470 BC, roughly a millennium after Giza.

facts.text: The statue was found intact inside Hatshepsut's temple.
facts.explanation: It had been smashed and dumped, and was reassembled from fragments in the 1920s.
